Executable protocols
--------------------

A protocol defines the control flow between native C hooks. It orders admission,
preparation, effects and ownership transfer, then emits an ordinary inline C
function. Hooks implement the domain-specific work; the protocol makes their
prerequisites and the exits of that work explicit.

  cesta protocol check MODULE THEORY
  cesta protocol plan MODULE THEORY -o PLAN
  cesta protocol export MODULE THEORY -o HEADER --plan PLAN --depfile DEPS
  cesta protocol verify MODULE THEORY -o HEADER --plan PLAN

verify regenerates and compares both artifacts byte for byte. It refuses changed
output even when the changed text is valid C. Exported definitions must occur
once per translation unit. Repeated protocol names are diagnosed, including
names introduced by separate imported modules; a later definition never silently
replaces or hides an earlier definition.

Declaration
-----------

  Module Example {
    Theory Protocols() {
      Empty Equations {
        (run) == (Protocol "cesta-protocol/1"
          (Context CallContext)
          (Hooks
            (Hook arity call_arity guard (Requires) (Uses) (Proves exact))
            (Hook prepare call_prepare prepare
              (Requires exact) (Uses frame) (Proves ready))
            (Hook execute call_execute effect
              (Requires ready) (Uses frame) (Proves)))
          (Resources (Resource frame frame_acquire frame_release frame_transfer
            (AcquireRequires exact) (TransferRequires ready)))
          (Entry (Facts) (Owns))
          (Body
            (Call arity
              (Acquire frame
                (Call prepare
                  (Call execute
                    (Release frame (Return answered))
                    (Release frame (Return raised)))
                  (Release frame (Return declined)))
                (Return resource_failure))
              (Return declined)))
          (Checks (Fact exact call_has_exact_arity)
                  (Fact ready call_is_ready)
                  (Own frame frame_is_owned)));
      }
    }
  }

The context is a C typedef. A Boolean hook takes Context * and returns bool.
Acquire has that signature too. Release and Transfer take Context * and return
void. Define the context and native functions before including the output.
Native declarations must be compatible with <stdint.h> and, for checked mode,
<stdio.h> and <stdlib.h>; include these before defining the native hooks. The
reader refuses callable names belonging to the C11 declarations used by these
headers, including diagnostic functions/streams and integer typedefs. Platform
extensions and the rest of the surrounding C namespace remain the compiler's
responsibility. Contexts may use an existing standard typedef.

guard inspects eligibility. prepare performs reversible preparation. effect may
commit an observable change, on either its true or false result. Requires lists
facts established on this path; Proves adds facts on the true path. Uses lists
resources whose tokens must be owned while the hook runs. An optional final
(Invalidates FACT...) list forgets certificates after that hook, on both true
and false branches. Requires is checked before forgetting; Proves then adds
certificates on the true branch. A write that may partly succeed before
reporting failure must invalidate its dependencies on that path too.

Invalidation forgets knowledge. It does not assert a false validator result,
change memory permissions, revoke another borrow or destroy an older immutable
snapshot. A subsequent hook must re-establish any required currentness fact.
Hooks must preserve certificates they do not invalidate; resource operations
must preserve certificates. Describe a mutating operation as a hook so its
invalidation is explicit. Native hook conformance remains an obligation.

Current.module demonstrates a mutation followed by revalidation before
publication. Omitting that revalidation is refused on either Boolean branch.

Statements
----------

  (Return OUTCOME)
  (Call HOOK TRUE-BRANCH FALSE-BRANCH)
  (Acquire RESOURCE ACQUIRED-BRANCH FAILURE-BRANCH)
  (Release RESOURCE NEXT)
  (Transfer RESOURCE NEXT)

Outcomes are declined, answered, done, raised, suspended, resource_failure and
engine_failure. done represents an ordinary completed computation, including an
empty answer. A failed match is not an allocation failure. The consuming runtime
chooses its explicit mapping from these outcomes to its own statuses.

Acquire succeeds with one new token; failure adds none. Release consumes the
token. Transfer consumes it and publishes responsibility to a receiving owner.
AcquireRequires and TransferRequires list facts required at those calls. Both
lists may be omitted together when neither native operation needs extra facts.
Declaring them prevents allocation before eligibility or publication before a
reservation has been validated. Release needs the live token and stays available
for cleanup even when a publication prerequisite fails.
All returns, including failure and suspension, must discharge every token.
Entry Owns can describe tokens supplied to a resumed boundary.

An optional (ExitRequires (OUTCOME FACT...) ...) clause declares certificates
required at each listed return. It may accompany Checks in either order.
Outcomes cannot repeat. Static checking requires the certificates on every
return path; checked execution re-observes them immediately before returning.
For example, (ExitRequires (suspended wake_registered) (answered result_ready))
refuses a pause without an established wake registration and an answer without
a completed result. Existing protocols without the clause retain their policy.

CallOnce.module demonstrates a shared logical call. Its effect requires a
permit which that effect invalidates on both Boolean outcomes. Later readers
must observe the saved result or establish a wake registration. The adapter
owns the persistent call identity, consumed-permit state and wake registry;
the generated protocol does not add a scheduler. Registration must bind the
same call and reader to a live completion source or finite timeout. A registered
obligation alone does not prove that an arbitrary scheduler eventually runs it.

Both effect calls and Transfer prohibit a later declined return. Acquire followed
by Release can still decline if the host implements it reversibly. A nested
protocol must inherit irreversible history from its caller; separately checking
two functions from an empty entry does not establish safe composition.

Rejected examples include preparation before its required arity fact, using a
resource before acquiring it, acquiring it twice, releasing it twice, leaking it
on failure, or transferring it before declining. Unknown hook kinds, outcomes,
resource names and repeated native identifiers are also refused.

Authoring and ordinary C
-----------------------

Inside a native-c/1 document, import the same protocol:

  (cesta native-c/1 compact-c/2
    (unit
      (include "local_hooks.h")
      (use-protocols "Example.module" Protocols)
      (fn int invoke ((CallContext (* context)))
        (return (== (call run context) run_answered)))))

cesta cc compiles the document with the selected C compiler. cesta export-c
writes its ordinary C representation and accepts --plan to record imported
protocol plans. The module filename is relative to the document. C compiler
dependency output includes the imported modules. Protocol imports occur at
translation-unit scope and may coexist with use-macros.

A project can keep the .cesta and .module definitions as its authoring source and
check in the generated C for users who build with GCC or Clang alone. Its optional
regeneration check needs Cesta; its ordinary C build does not need Lean or Cesta's
qualification suite.

Checked execution and decline counters
--------------------------------------

The optional final Checks clause maps facts and resource ownership to pure
Boolean predicates of Context *. Predicates observe the current state; they
must not prepare arguments, allocate, retain, release, mutate the context or
consume an external reply. They are distinct from the ordinary native hooks.
Every mapping must name a declared fact or resource, and mappings cannot repeat.

Define run_CHECKED to 1 before including a generated protocol named run to enable
validation. It checks Entry facts and each resource's declared initial ownership,
then checks each hook's Requires and Uses before calling it. Acquisition checks
its prerequisites and absence of ownership, then checks ownership against the
Boolean result. Release and Transfer require ownership, and must relinquish it.
Transfer also checks TransferRequires. Every return checks that no pending token
remains. A failed check prints the protocol, fact/resource and expected state,
then aborts before executing its continuation. NDEBUG does not disable this mode.
Missing required validators make checked compilation fail explicitly. Omitting
Checks remains supported for ordinary execution.

Facts are re-observed where they are required; guards are never replayed to
produce diagnostics. This catches a changed prerequisite before its next use,
but does not make arbitrary native predicates truthful or memory-safe.

Every declined return has a named run_decline_reason: run_declined_at_entry, or
run_declined_after_NATIVE_true/false for the latest Boolean control decision.
Void cleanup preserves that reason. A declined return records one event; other
returns record none. These are reasons for declining a route, not necessarily
the semantic cause of a failure inside the native hook.

By default, counting is disabled and no counter storage is allocated. To use the
generated saturating uint64_t helper with a private counter bank:

  struct run_counters;
  typedef struct CallContext {
      struct run_counters *diagnostics;
      /* application fields */
  } CallContext;
  #define run_COUNT_DECLINE(ctx, reason) \
      run_count_decline((ctx)->diagnostics, reason)
  #include "run.generated.h"

After inclusion, run_counters is a complete type. Its declines array is indexed
by run_decline_reason, with run_decline_count entries (or one unused slot when
no branch declines). The helper exists when counting is enabled and the protocol
has a decline. It ignores a null bank or invalid index and saturates at
UINT64_MAX. For the counted model, supply a valid private bank and use this
helper exactly once per macro invocation. A custom override's effects are not
covered by that model. Shared banks need synchronization supplied by the caller;
ordinary counter writes are not atomic. Checked mode and counting are separate.

With both disabled, focused controls require byte-identical complete objects
against ordinary C at -O0 and -O2 under GCC and Clang.

Evidence and boundary
---------------------

The exported plan records the authored protocol and an independently emitted
target tree of Return, IfCall and VoidCall. MeTTapedia's ExecutableProtocol model
checks the protocol and equality of that target with its separate lowering.
The source and target interpreters are independent. The simulation theorem
preserves the exact result, arbitrary host state, ordered repeated native calls,
Boolean replies consumed and the unconsumed suffix.

Instrumentation is recorded separately, including its validator mappings and
the actual Validate/Tick target. Missing mappings produce Unavailable rather
than a checked target. ExecutableProtocolInstrumentation and its correctness
module independently lower and interpret these nodes. Successful checked
execution projects to the same ordinary execution; a failed validation stops
before its continuation. Disabled nodes perform no observations or counter
updates. Counter state is separate from the host state, and the laws distinguish
one decline event from its saturating numeric update. The admission gate checks
actual emitted instrumentation against this lowering and refuses changed
validators, expectations, branches, tick reasons, missing checks and extra ticks.

ExecutableProtocolSafety proves prerequisite and ownership discipline on every
enabled trace, discharged tokens at every return and absence of publication on
decline. ExecutableProtocolComposition proves finite continuation substitution,
trace/state concatenation and additive event charges, retaining prior charges
on failure and suspension. Concrete token handoff requires an explicit host
ownership relation and conformance to it. Equal resource names are not evidence
that two boundaries transfer the same physical owner.

test-protocol-admission has the kernel decide actual recorded plans and reject
altered targets. test-protocols independently interprets authored declarations
and compares outcomes, host state and ordered traces with compiled exports under
GCC and Clang. It also tests authoring, dependency output and malformed inputs.

The model does not establish native hook purity, truth of native facts, physical
token exclusivity, allocator behavior, printed-C fidelity or compiler correctness.
Those remain implementation obligations. A declaration cannot make an arbitrary
C handler obey them. Event charges are a specified accounting observation, not a
claim about physical instructions, wall time, retained bytes or termination of a
native hook. Protocol bodies are finite; hooks may still diverge or suspend.

Operation contracts describe operation footprints, demand and policy. Executable
protocols define sequencing. There is no automatic inference that a hook obeys
an operation declaration, and an unknown footprint never establishes purity.

Bounded iteration
-----------------

  (Loop 64 BODY EXHAUSTED)
  (Loop (Limit budget) BODY EXHAUSTED)
  (Continue)

Loop snapshots its bound once and executes BODY at most that many times.
Continue starts the next iteration of the nearest enclosing loop. Return exits
the protocol. Exhaustion executes EXHAUSTED; that branch is part of the checked
protocol, so timeout cleanup and its outcome are explicit. Nested loops are
supported. Continue outside a loop is refused.

A literal is a canonical decimal integer in the uint64_t range. A field bound
names a nonvolatile uint64_t (or const uint64_t) context member; generated C
checks the actual member type. A hook changing that member does not change the
snapshot. The exporter emits a countdown, not a copy of BODY for every step.

Every Continue must preserve the loop entry's exact set of resource tokens and
at least its facts. It cannot silently drop a pending request or DMA buffer.
The conservative checker treats entering a loop as committed history, even
when its bound is zero; declining after a loop is refused. Exhaustion and all
other returns must discharge pending tokens. The bound counts iterations,
not elapsed time or the internal work of a native hook. Bounded completion
therefore requires the hooks themselves to return.

Checked mode re-observes entry facts and ownership at Continue. A freestanding
program may define run_CHECK_FAILURE(ctx, kind, id, expected) before importing
the protocol. The hook must stop execution; if it returns, generated code
remains in a nonreturning loop rather than executing an unchecked continuation.
Without an override, the default prints the failed check and aborts. Validators
must be pure and truthful in either configuration.

protocols/Wait.module gives a bounded request wait with explicit transfer on
completion and release on failure or timeout. A DMA timeout instead commonly
transfers the obligation to a failed-device quarantine: timing out is not proof
that hardware has stopped accessing its buffer.

The bounded source calculus and independently defined call/branch/countdown
calculus have equal executions, including calls, results, state and replies.
Lean also proves checker equivalence to the inductive formation rules, the
iteration bound, owner preservation at continuation and successful checked-run
erasure. tests/protocol_loop_admission.py checks the actual recorded ordinary
and instrumented targets and refuses altered targets. Native hooks, C text
printing and compilation remain separate obligations; this is not a proof of
arbitrary C hooks or a general borrow checker.
